steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Injection moulding: thermoplastic melted and forced into a steel mould under high pressure - mass production, high tooling cost, very low per-unit cost, complex 3D shapes. Used for LEGO bricks, bottle caps, phone cases.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: CNC machining: computer-controlled cutting from solid stock - precision, prototyping and batch production, no mould cost, but slower per unit and creates waste (swarf).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Blow moulding: extruded polymer tube inflated against a mould - produces hollow shapes (bottles). Extrusion: continuous profile pushed through a die - pipes, window frames.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Metal forming: press forming (sheet metal pressed between die and punch - car body panels), die casting (molten metal forced into a mould), sand casting (sand mould for one-offs/small batches).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain why injection moulding is used for mass-producing a polypropylene food container but not for a one-off prototype. | Compare CNC machining and 3D printing for producing a small batch (50 units) of a complex bracket prototype. | Describe the process of blow moulding a PET drinks bottle, explaining why this process is suitable for hollow containers.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always link the manufacturing process to the production volume - this is the key selection criterion Name the material AND the process together - 'injection moulded polypropylene' not just 'moulded' Know the difference between shaping (adding form) and cutting (removing material)
